nameStory: The "orange day-lily" gets its name from its vibrant orange petals and the fact that each gorgeous flower blooms for just one day before fading away. Despite being called a "lily," it's not actually related to true lilies at all - the name comes from the similar trumpet-shaped flowers that reminded people of lily blooms.
description: Orange day-lily is a hardy perennial plant that forms clumps of long, arching green leaves that fountain out from the base. In summer, tall flower stalks rise 3-4 feet high, topped with clusters of showy orange trumpet-shaped flowers. Each flower is about 4 inches across with six curved petals that flare outward, and though individual blooms last only a day, new ones keep opening for weeks. The plant spreads by underground stems to form large colonies over time.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright orange trumpet-shaped blooms with six curved petals that feel slightly waxy to the touch, each flower lasting exactly one day before wilting

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow leaves that arch gracefully like fountain spray, smooth to the touch with prominent parallel veins running lengthwise

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense clumps that spread outward, with flower stalks rising 3-4 feet above the foliage mass

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Plump, elongated flower buds clustered at stalk tips, feeling firm and slightly ridged when gently squeezed

habitat: Commonly found along roadsides, in ditches, and near old homesteads throughout New England, thriving in both sun and partial shade. It tolerates poor soils and drought conditions, often naturalizing in disturbed areas, field edges, and abandoned lots. Originally planted in gardens, it has escaped cultivation and established wild populations in many areas.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge early, forming fresh clumps of arching foliage. Flower stalks begin developing in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from June through August, with fresh orange flowers opening each morning and fading by evening. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Foliage remains green well into fall before gradually yellowing. Seed pods may form but plants mainly spread by underground stems.
seasonality.winter: Leaves die back completely, leaving only dormant underground root systems until spring emergence.

funFact: Orange day-lilies are like nature's daily gift shop - each flower bloom lasts exactly 24 hours, opening fresh in the morning and closing forever by nightfall, but a single plant can produce over 200 flowers in one season!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with true lilies, but day-lilies have fountain-like leaf clumps growing from the ground while true lilies have leaves growing up the flower stem itself. Remember: "Day-lily leaves spray from the base, true lily leaves climb the case."
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name, orange day-lily isn't related to true lilies at all - it's actually in the aloe family! This Asian native has so many colorful common names (ditch lily, outhouse lily, railroad lily) that reflect where people commonly see it growing wild.
compareHints: Orange day-lily is much more common than its relative yellow daylily in New England. Yellow daylily blooms earlier with pale yellow, very fragrant flowers, while orange day-lily blooms later with bright orange, nearly scentless flowers. Orange day-lily also forms much larger, more aggressive colonies than its yellow cousin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Yellow daylily is much rarer than its robust orange relative, the orange day-lily, which has completely taken over roadsides and fields across New England.
